Historically, the policy of abolishing Native American reservations and enforcing cultural assimilation—most prominently pursued during the late 19th century (the Allotment Era) and again in the mid-20th century (the Termination Era)—was supported by a mix of government officials, social reformers, and land speculators.

While these policies are now widely criticized for their devastating impact on Indigenous cultures and sovereignty, their supporters at the time framed them as "progressive" solutions to what was then called the "Indian Problem."

The following is an overview of the arguments and supposed benefits cited by proponents of these policies.

1. The Promotion of Individualism and Private Property

The central philosophy behind the Dawes Act of 1887 (General Allotment Act) was that communal land ownership was an obstacle to progress. Supporters believed that the Western concept of private property was the "civilizing" force necessary to transform Native Americans into productive citizens.

  • Economic Independence: Proponents argued that by giving individual Native Americans their own plots of land (usually 160 acres), they would learn the "value of work" and become self-sufficient farmers.
  • The "Jeffersonian" Ideal: Reformers believed that the agrarian lifestyle was the highest form of citizenship. They argued that breaking up tribal lands would force a transition from a hunting-and-gathering or communal lifestyle to one based on the individual nuclear family and capitalistic competition.

2. Legal and Social Equality (The "Citizenship" Argument)

Many supporters, including a group known as the "Friends of the Indian," viewed the reservation system as a form of segregation that kept Native Americans in a state of permanent "wardship" under the federal government.

  • Full Citizenship: Proponents argued that as long as Native Americans lived on sovereign reservations, they were denied the full rights and responsibilities of American citizens. Abolishing the reservation system was framed as a path toward legal equality.
  • Ending Dependency: Supporters believed the reservation system fostered a cycle of dependency on government rations and annuities. They argued that assimilation would allow Native Americans to enter the American workforce and contribute to the national economy.

3. Cultural "Uplift" and Modernization

During the late 19th century, many reformers believed that Indigenous cultures were "primitive" and destined to disappear in the face of industrial modernity. They viewed assimilation as a humanitarian effort to "save" individuals by erasing their cultural identity.

  • The "Kill the Indian, Save the Man" Philosophy: Captain Richard Henry Pratt, founder of the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, famously argued that the only way to help Native Americans survive was to strip them of their languages, religions, and traditions.
  • Education as a Tool: Supporters argued that boarding schools would provide Native children with the vocational skills, English language proficiency, and Christian moral framework necessary to navigate mainstream American society successfully.

4. National Unity and Administrative Efficiency

From a bureaucratic and political perspective, many government officials viewed the existence of "nations within a nation" as a legal and administrative nightmare.

  • Eliminating Special Status: During the Termination Era (1940s–1960s), proponents argued that Native Americans should no longer be subject to different laws or receive different services than other citizens. Senator Arthur V. Watkins, a leading advocate for termination, likened it to the Emancipation Proclamation, arguing it "freed" Native Americans from federal supervision.
  • Reducing Costs: The federal government sought to reduce the expense of managing tribal affairs and fulfilling treaty obligations. By dissolving tribes and selling "surplus" reservation land, the government aimed to simplify the national map and integrate reservation land into the tax base of the various states.
